sources.title: Ellison G, Jones M, Cain B, et al. (2024 issue; first published online 2023). Activity Budget and Sociality of the Northern Lesser Galago, Galago senegalensis. International Journal of Primatology 45:1538–1563.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods; Results; Discussion; Rights and permissions.
sources.scope: Primary study of activity budgets at Kwakuchinja, Tanzania, with group-size surveys at Fongoli, Senegal, and Lolldaiga Hills Ranch, Kenya. Sites used different group-size sampling methods.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, confirmed on the publisher page.
sources.attribution: Ellison G, Jones M, Cain B, et al. Activity Budget and Sociality of the Northern Lesser Galago, Galago senegalensis. International Journal of Primatology 45:1538–1563 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10764-023-00406-2. First published online 2023-11-06. Claims are paraphrased; no figures or tables are reproduced.

claims.text: At Kwakuchinja, 140 focal follows totaling 31.4 hours were analyzed; activity differed by time of night, with foraging more prevalent in the evening and inactivity higher in the morning.
claims.scope: Activity observations came from one Tanzanian population during dry-season field periods in 2016 and 2017.

claims.text: Group-size records showed two or more galagos in 55% of 76 Kwakuchinja encounters, whereas 79% of 185 Fongoli records and 80% of 142 Lolldaiga records were solitary. Vocalization rates were higher in the morning and contact calls relatively more frequent in the evening.
claims.scope: The three sites used different methods; the contrast is not a clean estimate of species-wide social organization.

claims.text: The authors describe population differences in observed sociality as preliminary and note that there is more to learn about the drivers of social structure.
claims.scope: Interpretive scope follows the paper conclusion; no causal drivers are established.

gaps: No multi-source species dossier is added.
Activity-budget data come from one Tanzanian site and dry-season observations; the other site records use different methods.
The study does not establish species-wide social organization, diet, population trends, full distribution, or formal conservation status.
